segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When we were weak, we told ourselves we were strong. And sometimes, if we were very weak, we told ourselves we were very, very strong.

segments.speaker: Chris Ware
segments.text: I mean unquestionably, I was by far the most loathed member of my class, I think, you know? Being a pasty, unathletic kid who was weird looking and probably seemed overly eager, so, you know. And I had friends that would come over on the weekends to play. But then at school, they would ignore me and pretend like they didn't know me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so when he was little, Chris Ware-- the guy you were just hearing-- spent a lot of time thinking about superpowers. He drew superheroes over and over, trying to get them right. He always wondered where somebody could find a radioactive animal like the one that bit Peter Parker and turned him into the amazing Spider-Man. And a couple of times, Chris thought that he might be developing his own superpowers-- real ones.

segments.speaker: Chris Ware
segments.text: There was one morning where I was standing under the shower. And of course, when you get in immediately because you're so cold, the water is extremely hot by contrast. So you have the cold water turned up. And as you stand in there, you get used to it, and you turn the cold water down.

segments.speaker: Chris Ware
segments.text: And I was in there for a very long time. And I remember turning the cold, and it wouldn't go any farther. And I thought, well, that's weird. It must be stuck. And I turned it more, and it wouldn't go any farther. And I realized I was standing under completely hot water, but it felt fine to me. It actually felt warm, almost cool.

segments.speaker: Chris Ware
segments.text: And the longer I stood there, it felt cooler and cooler. And the only explanation I could come up with is that I had developed the ability to withstand extraordinary heat. And, of course, we'd just run out of hot water. But at that time, I didn't know that that happened. I thought hot water was an endless commodity.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He invented his own superhero called the Hurricane, who could shoot blasts of wind from his hands and was drawn with huge, manly muscles. He made a Hurricane costume that he could wear himself-- red t-shirt with a black circle with an H on it, and a mask that his mom made for him, and a yellow cape. You know, some kids really go for a cape.

segments.speaker: Chris Ware
segments.text: There were a few times where I actually came to school with bits of a superhero costume secreted under my school uniform. I don't exactly know why. I guess I thought it was like it was going to give me some sense of power or something. But of course, then I have gym class, you know? So you have to change your clothes, so I don't know what I was thinking.

segments.speaker: Chris Ware
segments.text: There was one time I actually-- this is sort of peripherally superhero, but I'd actually drawn circuit boards on pieces of paper, like the Bionic Man, the $6 Million Man. And I'd actually taped them on my legs to look like real circuitry exposed, as if I had mechanical legs or something like that. So I guess I vaguely thought that somebody would catch a glimpse of it and think, wow. Look. He's bionic,

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Some of us, we spend a long, long time hoping that we're more than what the world thinks of us. And so of course we're drawn to these stories of these mild-mannered guys who, underneath their clothes, wear a costume in secret with powers nobody suspects. And when we get older, it all seems ridiculous, of course. It seems really, really dumb. It's embarrassing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Chris Ware, though, went on to draw cartoons for his living. But the cartoons that he draws are like novels. They're graphic novels about real people. And anytime a Superman type shows up in one of his cartoons, he's always somebody trying to con kids with a costume and a cape. He's always a disappointment.

segments.speaker: Chris Ware
segments.text: It's just more interesting that way. I think he's more like a real dad that way, I guess. And the more I draw him, the fatter he gets too, and the more bald he gets, I guess.

segments.speaker: Chris Ware
segments.text: I mean, if you were Superman, too, you're like-- you know, what do you care what you look like? You wouldn't be all handsome. You'd just eat whatever you felt like. You'd take whatever you wanted. And you'd end up looking really terrible after a while, I think. If I was a superhero, I think I would probably-- I mean, who's going to criticize you?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, today on our radio program, superpowers-- four real life stories about how easy it is to be caught up in the dream of them. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira. Glass. As the super-villains say, silence, miscreant. Our program has begun.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, The Invisible Man Vs. Hawkman.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So we now present a kind of super contest for you, beloved super listener, between two ancient superpowers-- two of the superpowers which have fascinated humans since antiquity. And actually, this is kind of a super Rorschach test. John Hodgman has been conducting an unscientific survey, posing for people a very simple choice.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Flight versus invisibility. This question is only for you. Whichever you pick, you'll be the only person in the world to have that particular superpower. You can't have both. Which do you choose? I started wondering about this a few years ago. I'd bring it up at parties, dinners, wedding receptions. It was more interesting to ask than where people worked or where they went to school and clearly more fun to answer.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Like a magic word, shazam, flight versus invisibility would instantly change an evening's character, opening passionate conversation and debate. But what surprised me more was how quickly everyone would choose, as though they had been thinking about it for a long time. Everyone knew exactly which superpower they wanted and what they would do with it. Their plans weren't always flashy or heroic. In fact, they almost never were.

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: If I could fly, the first thing I would do is fly into the bar, check out what's going on there, fly back home. I would attach my baby to me and fly to a doctor's appointment at 11:30 and fly right back. Then I think I would fly to Atlantic City.

segments.speaker: Man 2
segments.text: I would imagine if it got around that I had the power of flight, and it was a rare type of thing, I mean, there would definitely be flight groupies. I would imagine. So there's going to be just, like, oh, yeah. I just slept with a flying dude. You know? But people are just like, oh, score.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I'd go into Barney's. I'd pick out the cashmere sweaters that I like. I'd go into the dressing room. The woman says, how many items? I say five. I go into the dressing room. I put those five sweaters on, and I summon my powers of invisibility in the dressing room. I turn invisible. I walk out, leaving her to wonder why there's a tag hanging from the door that says five and no person inside.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: So you would become a thief pretty quickly?

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Immediately, until I had all the sweaters that I wanted. And then I would have to think of other things to do.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Typically, this is how it goes. People who turn invisible will sneak into the movies or onto airplanes. People who fly stop taking the bus. Here's one thing that pretty much no one ever says. I would use my power to fight crime. No one seems to care about crime.

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: I don't think I would want to spend a lot of time using my power for good. I mean, if I don't have super strength, and I'm not invulnerable, then, I mean, would be very dangerous. If you had to. rescue somebody from a burning building or something like that, you might catch on fire.

segments.speaker: Man 2
segments.text: Just having flight I don't think is necessarily quite enough because you don't have the super strength.

segments.speaker: Man 3
segments.text: I'd still be weak when I got there, I guess. I don't fight crime now, and people without superpowers do. So sure, in theory, yes. But I'm not a-- I mean, what can I do as a-- I mean, either one of those-- you see, you need a whole package because there's not much you can do with any one thing. I'd go to Paris, I suppose.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: That's not being a super hero.

segments.speaker: Man 3
segments.text: Well, may-- you know, I could be a Going-to-Paris Man, that sort of a superhero.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Going-to-Paris Man is not a superhero. And I have to say this drove me crazy a little bit. We are, after all, talking about superpowers. Why not take down organized crime, bring hope to the hopeless, swear vengeance on the underworld, if only a little bit?

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: I proposed a variety of sample scenarios along these lines, such as, how would you handle a mad genius taking over the Empire State Building or a group of terrorists hijacking an overseas flight? And what I learned is some people should simply not be fighting crime.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Well, the first thing that occurs to me is I'd go sneak up behind them very low and with a knife that they didn't see and slice their Achilles tendon. Uh, no. I somehow shove a sock in their mouth, or something like that, and wrap some tape around their mouth so that they can't yell out. It might not be a sock. It might just be some napkins or something. I can't keep all this in my head. I'd have to keep a bag full of stuff with me-- [LAUGHS] knives, socks, tape.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Do you think you would be tempted to enlist a teenage helper?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: No, I think a helper would be good, a helper with a complimentary power.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: There's no others-- anybody else with superpowers.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Oh. It would just be a teenager hanging around me? No.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: People who consider invisibility always want to know, do I have to be naked? People who choose flight want to know how fast. Almost all asked, who would win in a fight, Mr. Invisible or Flying Man? And so I had to lay down some rules.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Invisibility means the power to become transparent at will, including your clothing, but anything you may pick up is visible. Flight means the power to fly at any altitude within the Earth's atmosphere at speeds up to 1,000 miles per hour. But even then they start looking for loopholes, hidden catches, superpower fine print. They start negotiating their dreams with me.

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: Now, when you're flying, if you're flying at 1,000 miles an hour at 100,000 feet, are you comfortable? Do you get very cold?

segments.speaker: Man 2
segments.text: Let's say I'm in this room, and I'm invisible. And I'm walking around this apartment, and I'm invisible. And--

segments.speaker: Man 3
segments.text: Yes, you--

segments.speaker: Man 2
segments.text: Do I have to be completely quiet or you guys will hear my footsteps?

segments.speaker: Man 3
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Man 2
segments.text: Because that's a pain in the ass. And also someone would have to let you in.

segments.speaker: Man 4
segments.text: Can I carry somebody? Can somebody go on my back?

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Can you carry someone on your back now?

segments.speaker: Man 4
segments.text: Little people, yeah.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Then you can carry little people on your back.

segments.speaker: Man 4
segments.text: Done. Flight, it is.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: This is all part of what I call the five stages of choosing your superpower. Sometimes, this process occurs in just moments. For example, subject A, a tallish man with glasses wedged into a cramped bar room corner begins as they all do, with stage 1-- gut reaction.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Initially, I would think perhaps invisibility.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Next comes stage 2-- practical consideration.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Because you have the ability to walk around work, perhaps, show up at one point and perhaps go away for a little while and turn invisible, and then come back and listen to what they say about you. You have the power to spy on your exes, and that would all be enlightening, and fun, and in fact, a little bit perverted.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: You hear that doubt in his voice? That's the beginning of stage 3-- philosophical reconsideration.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That would-- I believe it would be-- it would immediately turn into a life of complete depression. You wouldn't be able to really share with anyone, you know? And I know there would be some problems with the perversion thing.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Stage 4-- self-recrimination.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Invisibility leads me, as an invisible person, down a dark path, because you're not going want to miss out when you're invisible on-- you know, no matter how many times you've seen a woman naked in a shower, you're going to want to see it again because there's always a different woman, right? And there's just like a lifetime of that. And that's not acceptable behavior, no matter whether you're invisible or not.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: And finally, stage 5-- acceptance.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yeah. I'd have to go with flight.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: So who chooses invisibility, and who chooses flight? In my experience, though there are lots of exceptions, men lean toward flying, women to invisibility. And many brood anxiously over their choice, switching from one to the other and back again. And that's because more than the ability, say, to burst into flame or shoot arrows with uncanny accuracy, flight and invisibility touch a nerve. Actually, they touch two different nerves, speak to very different primal desires and unconscious fears.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: My friend Christine chose invisibility.

segments.speaker: Christine
segments.text: One superpower is about something that's obvious, and the other is about something that is hidden. I think that indicates your level of shame.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: How do you mean?

segments.speaker: Christine
segments.text: A person who chooses to fly has nothing to hide. A person who'd choose to be invisible wants clearly to hide themselves.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Do you feel that you want to hide yourself?

segments.speaker: Christine
segments.text: I want to-- I'd like to not-- I'm not going to answer that question.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: It all has to do with guile. Wanting to be invisible means that you're a more guileful person. If you want to fly, it means you're guileless. And I think the reason that I'm so conflicted about flying versus invisibility is that I have guile, but I really wish that I didn't.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Flight is the hero-- selfless, and competent, and unashamed. And invisibility, the villain. Almost everyone I talked to called invisibility the sneakier power.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Flying is for people who want to let it all hang out. Invisibility is for fearful, crouching masturbators.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: First of all, I think that a lot of people are going to tell you that they would choose flight. And I think they're lying to you. I think they're saying that because they're trying to sound all mythic and heroic, because the better angels of our nature would tell us that the real thing that we should strive for is flight and that that's noble and all that kind of stuff. But I think actually, if everybody were being perfectly honest with you, they would tell you the truth, which is that they all want to be invisible so that they can shoplift, get into movies for free, go to exotic places on airplanes without paying for airline tickets, and watch celebrities have sex.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Anyone faced with this choice in their heart of hearts will choose invisibility?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yes, or they have this sort of inflated, heroic, mythical concept of themselves, and that in fact, they're not really giving it very much practical thought.

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: In the end, it's not a question of what kind of person flies and what kind of person fades. We all do both. Perhaps that's why, when I put the choice to myself, I'm hopelessly, completely stuck. At the heart of this decision the question I really don't want to face is this-- who do you want to be? The person you hoped to be, or the person you fear you actually are?

segments.speaker: John Hodgman
segments.text: Don't rush into it. Think it over. Which would you choose?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: John Hodgman is the author of many fine books. His latest is called Vacationland: True Stories from Painful Beaches.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [MUSIC - "THAT MAN" BY PEGGY LEE]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Two, Wonder Woman.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. What are the ways to create a superhero? Gamma rays, space alien abduction, prison experiment, or a NASA flight gone awry. And then there's the idea of a list. Is it possible that a to-do list is powerful enough to achieve this incredible result? Hmm. Kelly McEvers met somebody who tried.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: We met in a bar in Flagstaff, Arizona. I'd just moved back from Cambodia, and I was going out for one of my first beers back in the States.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Not long into the first one, I noticed this Amazon of a woman with huge blond and red-streaked hair and frosty lips, wearing a short, red tank dress and at least 50 bracelets. She's six feet tall and showing a lot of leg. People at the bar swivel their heads to watch her every move.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: She stands next to me to order a drink and in this throaty voice says, what are those? Pointing to my cigarettes. I tell her they're Cambodian. Her eyes light up, and she shoots out a long, tanned arm and points at a table in the corner. She orders me there. Before I can say no, I'm following her to my seat.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: She tells me she's an international private investigator, a bounty hunter, and a bail bonds enforcer, and that her name is Zora. I sit there for hours listening to her.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Within a week, she takes me to Las Vegas. We drive there in her red Mustang. As always, there's a Colt .380 under the driver's seat and a .45 Megastar in the trunk. In Vegas, we skip the casinos and head straight for the male strip clubs where Zora drops at least $200 on lap dances from buff guys with names like Roman.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Her get-up is the same as before-- teased hair, jewelry, and the ubiquitous tank dress-- which, I realize, is the best way to show off her tattoos. One is this big circle with blue and white swirls in it, kind of like a bowling ball on her left shoulder. Every guy she meets asks her about it. And when they hear her answer, they sometimes propose marriage.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Turns out the tattoo is a magic globe she holds in her dreams. And in these dreams, it gives her superpowers.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Ever since I remember, I've had the dreams. And they're very vivid, but it varies. It usually involves fighting, sometimes with guns, sometimes with superhero powers-- lightning from my fists, and all that. And I usually have super strength, and I can fly, and I have all those things, right?

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: And it's my most common set of dreams. And it varies. Sometimes it's medieval. Sometimes it's futuristic. Sometimes it's like a guerrilla war in Latin America.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Can you describe that Zora to me? The Zora in the dreams?

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Very powerful athletically, but beyond the rules of nature that this world allows. So 6'5" and long-- like almost impossibly long silver hair. This sort of otherworldly quality to her where her voice did not sound normal. It sounded almost musical.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: It became something that I aspire to be-- aspire to be this sort of superhero, this sort of person who would fight for a cause. Yeah. It was my motivation in life. Ever since I was 10 or 11, I decided that that was my goal.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Zora took the dreams seriously. So seriously that, at the age of 12, she sat down and composed a list of some 30 skills she needed to learn if she wanted to become as close to a superhero as any mortal could be. She even gave herself a deadline-- to master these skills by the time she was 23.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: I know it's in these.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Zora pulls out the old spiral notebook that was her diary at the age of 13 and turns to the inside back cover.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Yep. There's the list.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Wow. Why don't you go ahead and read it?

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: OK. The list included martial arts, electronics, chemistry, metaphysics, hang gliding, helicopter and airplane flying, parachuting, mountain climbing, survival--

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Throughout her teens and 20s--

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: --martial arts, politics--

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: --each time she started a new diary, she would update the list--

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: --physics--

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: --and write it in the back of the book.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: French, Arabic, Spanish--

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Each one with the same format, each one titled, The List.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Weaponry, rafting, scuba diving, herbology. Yes, I studied that. CPR, first aid and mountain emergency kind of medicine.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: The list also includes--

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Archaeology--

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: --bodybuilding, archery--

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: --sailing--

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: --demolitions, and explosives. She wanted to learn how to hunt animals and track men.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: This is funny. I have here major physical conditioning.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: And the most incredible thing about all of this is that Zora accomplished nearly every item on the list.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Throwing stars, and compound bows, and throwing knives, and-- yes. It was a very interesting pastime.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: To keep up with the goals set by the list, she sped through school. Starting in the seventh grade, she began completing entire school years during the summer term and finished high school by the time she was 15. She got her BA at 18, a masters at 20, and completed the coursework for a PhD in geopolitics by the time she was 21. She wanted to live like Indiana Jones, spending half her time in the classroom and half her time saving the world in the jungles of Peru.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Item number 4, camel, elephant riding. Evasive driving and stunts.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: When you're a kid, you have these romantic visions of what you'll be when you grow up. But how many people are so diligent they commit their dreams to paper and make it their life's work to achieve them? How many keep a list, amending it, adding to it, ticking things off as they go along well into their adult lives?

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: After finishing the coursework for her PhD, Zora decided to quit school, disappointed at the lack of cliff-hanging adventure in her doctoral program. And since superheroes who live in the real world need jobs, she decided to seek employment at the only place that would allow her to put all the skills from the list to use. Zora wanted to become an agent in the CIA. And so began a rigorous application process-- interviews, psych exams, a three-day lie detector test.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: After that, then they sent investigators out to interview me, interview my neighbors, interview ex-boyfriends, interview friends, ex-friends, former colleagues, people I work with, people I used to work with.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: They threw a question out in the middle of an interview. So what would you do in this situation? If you were driving down the road and you had one of your native agents with you, someone who's going to give you some information, and you were in a third-world country somewhere, and you were driving a car, and you accidentally ran into a dog? And people have been out playing in the street, children in the street, they see their dog get killed. And they get upset, and they rush towards the car. What do you do in that situation? You don't want to draw attention to the person who's with you.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: So what I said was that I would tell my agent to get down lower in the car. And I would get out of the car and draw the attention to myself and try to appease them in some way, either by giving them money, more likely, but-- and that was an acceptable answer to them. That was a good answer to them.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: At the time, when I was going through the process, it felt like everything was coming together. And I had not felt so much joy, probably ever.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Did you tell them about your dreams?

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Absolutely not. And I would tell them that I had a sense that I could combine the whole street smarts, intellectual, the education, with the sort of adventurer personality. And I was actually told that I had the perfect personality for it and that I would do really well. It was like the fruition of my life, that it was going to be the step into the next-- you know, where I would be using all that list and preparation for the next phase, which would be to actually put it into practice.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: About eight months into the interviews, Zora got a letter saying she'd been rejected. She appealed over the next year and a half, partly to find out why they'd turned her down. But the best they could do was to tell her to try again in a few more years. In the end, the CIA wouldn't take her, and they wouldn't even tell her why.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Probably it took me more like two years to recover. I was a basket case. I wasn't-- I wasn't-- I was just down, you know? I would have to work. I couldn't concentrate. Sort of slumped down, staring at the wall. I put my whole life into examination, all the years of preparation.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Most of us give up our dreams of superhero adventure when we're adolescents. Zora was only getting to it at the age of 27. Here she knew how to fly a helicopter and survive in the wilderness, but for what?

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: She devoted a lot of time to thinking about why she might have been rejected by the CIA. Maybe it was all those months she spent with right-wing militia groups doing her doctoral research. Maybe she shouldn't have told the CIA how she ended up in a clandestine IRA club one night while on vacation in Ireland. Maybe the CIA didn't like the fact that her father, a professor at the University of Minnesota, is an outspoken Serbian nationalist. Or maybe it was simply her own fault-- that she couldn't turn herself into a superhero.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: I had violated the agreement of the list, violated the agreement that I made with myself, that I had not become what the archetype was, that I had become something lacking. The point being that my mythology should have guided me better, and it felt like such a final thing.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: So Zora remade herself. She had been virtually isolated from other people since she was 15, when she started actively pursuing the goals on the list. Her parents were happy she was so busy because she had no time for boys. But now she started working for a woman private investigator.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: One day when she went to court, she wore her first pair of pantyhose because she was told it would help her look more feminine. Soon after, she was schooled in the sheer power of lipstick, a short skirt, and a supermodel runway walk to control the minds of others. These days, she works for an international private investigation agency that handles these kinds of cases.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Child abduction retrieval custody, reverse stings, occult and ritualistic crimes-- those tend to be really interesting, I like working on those-- anti-terrorism, kidnap protection and return, counterintelligence.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: She's happy doing this work. In a typical case, Zora's agency sent her on a mission to Mexico to do what's known as a reverse scam. The agency was hired by the family of a young woman who'd recently traveled there and fallen in love with a man she planned to marry after knowing him for only 10 days. The family suspected some sort of con.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Zora contacted him, pretending she was looking for a girlfriend who used to work with him in the travel industry. She took a photo of a classmate with her to begin the scam.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: I sort of played the distressed American student going to the Spanish school. And he invited me on a couple of dates and asked me to come back for the bullfight.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: What did you wear when you went to the bullfight?

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: Oh, I wore like a little, itty-bitty skirt and a little tank top.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: I made it seem like I had plenty of money, and that interested him. You know, he kind of perked up at that. He never mentioned, the whole time that I ever spent any time with him, he never mentioned that there was ever a woman. I found him to be pretty emotionally open and a very romantic guy, but I honestly felt that he probably was not in love with her, that he was taking this as an opportunity to live in the United States. And that was the report I gave.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: Before Zora set out for Mexico, I rode with her to the airport. We were late and hurrying through the terminal, just 10 minutes to spare, when she did the strangest thing. She sat down in a chair far from the gate and wouldn't move. I told her she was going to miss her flight, but she didn't budge.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: I sat down next to her. She said she was scared. About the case? About which disguise she might wear? About being found out? No, she said. She said she was afraid that when she got to Mexico, people wouldn't like her.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: The next time I was at her house, I hadn't noticed before, but I realized her bookshelf was packed with advice on how to build confidence-- titles like Princessa: Machiavelli for Women. Books like that aren't really so far from the idea of keeping a list, having an ongoing plan for self-improvement, believing that if you just put something on paper and stick to it, you can change.

segments.speaker: Zora
segments.text: I need to learn how to play tennis and golf. And my new list is windsurfing, tennis, golf. I need to develop some kind of talent. Like I need to learn how to sing properly, or to do some kind of comedy or sketches, acting. Acting-- I need to learn how to act. Oh, I need to learn how to sing like Billie Holiday.

segments.speaker: Kelly Mcevers
segments.text: She doesn't take the list so seriously these days. There are no deadlines. She puts things on the list and later decides not to do them. It's not a grand mission anymore. Now, it's just a list.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Kelly McEvers-- she's the host of NPR's Embedded podcast. Zora is currently doing a kind of superhero work. She's on the UN peacekeeping mission-- no kidding-- in the Central African Republic.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our program, of course, we choose a theme, bring you a variety of different kinds of stories on that theme. Today's program-- superpowers and how easy it is to get caught up in the dream of superpowers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We've arrived at Act Three. Act Three-- The Green Team of Superhero Boy Millionaires, the Amazing Super Monkey From Planet Krypton, and the Man From Sram. My friends, they come in waves-- 100 a year or more, whole armies of them. I'm talking about new superheroes created by the comic book companies. It is rare for any of them to last more than a few issues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The website Gone and Forgotten is, as far as we can tell, the authoritative archive of these failed super souls. The guy who runs the site under the title Your Humble Editor is Jonathan Morris. He says that the few great superheroes have some common sense things going for them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One, they have powers that make intuitive sense. Two, they have a reason for fighting crime. Three, the stories have a human touch to them. You can relate to them. He agreed to come into the studio with a stack of some of the comics that do not quite measure up to those super standards.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: I'm trying to find a very good one. I've brought a ton of comics with me. Let's see. We've got Captain Marvel, who's one of the characters featured on the website. His amazing power is that he can split, by which we mean his limbs fall off and then flail around. Hopefully, I imagine, beating up the criminal.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: I'm not kidding. He says, split. His arms, legs, and head fall off, and he screams, yow, I popped apart! And with the word, zam, he returns to normal.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's a--

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: He's flying into action.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I don't even know why-- that is one of the most disturbing things I've ever heard.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: This company had a number of characters who shared their names with preexisting characters. They had a Plastic Man, who appeared in this very issue, in fact, but he was nothing like the famous Plastic Man.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which was always an embarrassment to him. He'd be ordering-- you know, he'd be ordering online, or he'd--

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: He gets his mail all the time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Exactly. He'd make a reservation at a restaurant. And then he'd show up, and they're like, oh, we thought you were the other Plastic Man.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: Right. And there's even a point where he hears people yell Plastic Man on the street, and he's long past the point where he's thinking, maybe they mean me. No, he knows they mean the guy in the red.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: I did bring all the Preses with me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Pres?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: Pres-- the first teen president of the United States. A rather earnest young man named Pres Rickard becomes-- and with a name like that, how could he not? He becomes the first teenage president of the United States.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: This is the issue right before he has to fight vampires too, which was not a responsibility I was aware the president had, but apparently it's rather important.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, what is his superpower? Like what kind of president does he make?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: Well, he kind of fits in that Doc Savage, Batman mold where he's mostly a very well-trained human. And thanks to his Indian companion Eaglefree's menagerie of animals, he learns several animal skills-- helping teach Pres Rickard how to be fast as an antelope, swing like a monkey, fight like a bear, I guess.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You know, I've always thought that the United States presidency would be so much more effective if the president had the powers to communicate and control the animals.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: Well, there's one thing that Pres proves. It's that there's nothing that the President couldn't solve with two fists, an Indian companion, and a small army of birds and elephants.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: If you were to explain to people the characteristics of a bad comic book superhero--

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: Yeah. There are obviously a lot of ways you can screw up. One of the ways is to just overdo it and cram the elements of the character down the readers' throats.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: One of the characters was Bee Man, and everything about him was bees. His full name was Barry E. Eames. He was attacked by mutant bees which were sent to Earth by space alien bee people. And he himself became a mutant bee person who had bee powers, and lived in a hive, and ate honey, and stole gold because gold looked like honey. And he could sting you.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: There's nothing bee-related this man refused to do. It's as if you meet somebody at a bar, you start talking to him, and you realize he only has one interest in life. That's exactly what Bee Man was. Everything would have gotten back to bees. You start talking about what you watched on television last night, he'll say, you know, I saw an interesting show on bees.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do certain comic superheroes come out of particular moments in the nation's history?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: Positively. That's another thing that really works against a character is when they're tied in too tightly to a fad or tied in too tightly to something that is identifying an era. There's a character created in the '70s, but who was supposed to be a retro character from the '50s, name of 3D Man, to help hook up on the 3D movies that were a craze in the '50s. Terrible, flat character. Nothing going on.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And when you say 3D Man, what was his power?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: He had a magical pair of glasses and had the strength of three men. And that's it. He was as strong as three people, fast as three people, whatever that means-- Probably three times faster than a human being.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: They always describe it as something as so much as three men. But I don't see how how he can be three times as-- or have the agility of three men. There's just three guys who are agile. It doesn't make any sense. I have a little trouble with 3D Man.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: Part of the problem with just naming off the superheroes or going through their powers is that, on the face value, there's not a superhero who doesn't seem silly. Because you have to get to a point where the man's wearing a costume, and he's driving around fighting crime.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then where does the line come where they rise above that? Do you have a theory on this about what makes a good one and a bad one?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: I have sort of a half-formed theory. I know that one of the things that really helps a superpower get over with the audience, get over with readers, is if it's something they can apply to their normal lives, perhaps by way of fantasy.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: And that's, I think, why super strength, super speed, invulnerability, or just general toughness are often so common. If you can get on the court with it, get that super accuracy and get a slam dunk from midcourt and really just school over somebody, then that's probably a superpower you want. But when you start getting into powers, like one character who had magnetic eyes of superpower, which is a little too esoteric to even understand--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. I don't even understand anything you say.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What does it mean? Magnetic eyes of super power?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Morris
segments.text: But yeah, in his first appearance, he announced that he had magnetic eyes of superpower. They would illustrate little beams coming out of his eyes making metal things shoot right at them, which would be terrible in a room full of forks.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jonathan Morris, who brought a few of his 15,000 comics into the studio-- search the internet for Gone and Forgotten, and you'll find his web site.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Of course, you can't have a superhero without a supervillain. And the most interesting supervillains, of course, are the ones who think that they are the real heroes, that they're the ones living by a true code of honor, not the guys in the capes. This story comes from Glynn Washington.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: Rule number 1-- whatever it is you do, always look good doing it. See, now, my quantum drive, the lithium core, dimension jumping rocket ship, does not just go fast, it's sharp, baby. Yes, that is a new chrome alloy. And no, it is not available in stores. Recognize.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: And please understand, if they hadn't made the big fuss about how unbreakable the new security system was, I wouldn't even have bothered. Check the tape. I sat there for 45 minutes, big sack full of jewels in my lap before I finally pulled the alarm my damn self. That's when the fun started.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: I hopped in my rocket ship and tore through the middle of downtown Metropolis, making up all kinds of commotion-- sirens, helicopters, police lights. I'm having a ball. Then here he comes-- Superman. And right on cue, the ladies start screaming. Oh, Superman, Superman. Superman's so brave. It is not brave to go in the burning building when you do not burn. It ain't brave to get shot when you don't feel bullets. Superman-- nothing stops him. Nothing.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: Yeah, kryptonite-- please. I think he started that nonsense. I tried everything-- kryptonite rays, kryptonite missiles. Once, I had the fool locked in a kryptonite coffin. Oh, oh, it hurts. Kryptonite, kryptonite. Then he broke out and started tearing up my secret lab. It just never stops.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: Then-- then-- he's got the nerve to put on some glasses. And suddenly, he's incognito, like I'm stupid. I even called him out at the club. What's up, Superman? How you doing, Superman? Clark-- steady, looking all around all corny like I must be talking to somebody else. Excuse me? What's going on here? Whatever, man.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: And no, this had nothing to do with Lois Lane. You want to know what this is about? You want to know what this beef is about? One thing, and one thing only-- jungle fever.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: Superman had it bad. Call me what you want to, but Clark Kent was up in Lector's nightclub seven nights a week chasing the chocolate goodness. And I'm not hating. I understand.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: So one night, I'm ordering my Hennessy, turn around, and there he is talking to Sheila. My Sheila. And I went, oh, hell to the no. But I'm supposed to step to the Man of Steel?

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: And on top of everything else, Superman's got that mind control. How else Sheila going to get up in front of everybody in the club and walk out with Clark Kent? Explain me that. She was with me. She came there with me.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: So yeah, I stalked him. I followed him. I know him better than his Momma, and I don't know him at all. He's weird. Like he's reading the words that come out of his mouth. For a while, I thought he was a robot because everybody breaks character sometimes. But not Superman.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: I trailed him with my special Seeing Everywhere Machine. He knew I was watching him the whole time, and he didn't care. Why should he? Do you know what Superman does in his apartment by himself? Huh? Nothing. Just sits there. Doesn't turn on the TV. Doesn't eat cereal. Doesn't watch porn. He does nothing but sit there and look stupid.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: I had to take him out. I tried to take him out. I couldn't take him out. At first, if you don't succeed, try again, and again, and again. And every time, he's all flying me back to jail, steady, making pronouncements about fighting evil. I am nobody's evil. I just don't think we should be letting aliens from outer space roll up in here with our women. That's right, I said it-- our women. Now I'm evil? Please.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: My name is Darnell, and what I am is a student of the game. The rules clearly state when the big dog is up in your way, accept the play, son. Or-- or you go get you some more juice. I needed power-- crazy power, power like the sun.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: I started looking in my brand new secret laboratory. Turns out there are dimensions between the dimensions and dimensions between that. The deeper you dig, the stronger the force, the stronger the power. All this technology, and in the end, I didn't just find power, I found God, and I put him in a gun. At least, I think it's God. Or maybe it's the devil.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: It's really simple, though. At the end of the universe, the end of time, the end of everything, it is going to ask you what matters. No more waiting eons for your personal judgment day. My little shooter sends you there with a quickness, and you can't lie. You can't lie. God will have her answer.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: So anyway, Superman was hovering in front of my chrome grill rocket ship. I went on ahead and fired my tractor beam. Useless. Superman ripped the hatch off my ship like it was wrapping paper. All right. All right. You got me. Stop tearing up my ride.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: Your reign of terror has come to an end. The crowd cheered. Superman's gaze stayed fixed into the distance as he flew me off to prison. I even gave him a couple minutes. Hey, Clark? He didn't turn his head, didn't look at me. I was not worth the effort to him.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: Hey, Clark? I've got a present for you. I shot God right between his eyes. It was instantaneous. I saw Superman at the end of a universe. Then came the question. Will you give your life to save this world? Or will you live as a hero knowing the Earth is doomed?

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: Tough one, Clark. Lay down your life like a new Jesus, or keep up with this fake hero act. Superman bowed his head and answered instantly, softly, hero. (ECHO) Hero.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: Ah. Finally, at long last, Super Duper Man was off script. Then we were back in the sky, Superman still flying me off to jail. The air was warm, salty, delicious. I spoke in a little voice, because I know he's got that super hearing.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: Clark? Clark? I heard you, Clark. I heard you sell us out. Nothing. Nothing. No reaction at all. Then he blinked. Just a blink, and everything changed.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: We sped towards the ground. I didn't scream because I couldn't scream. I couldn't inhale. We landed, soft, like a swan kissing the water. He released me. His eyes shone. His mouth hung open in shock.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: Then Superman shrieked. The air burned. Yeah, he looked at me then. Yeah. For the first time ever, he looked at me then. I spit in his face. It ran down his cheek and his eye. He shot up into the air speeding toward the sun.

segments.speaker: Glynn Washington
segments.text: See? Life hurts. We all have hard choices to make. I had my own decision in front of the light. But that-- [CHUCKLES] see, that's a whole other story.
